sources.author: Épictète
sources.title: Manuel (Enchiridion), sections 1 et 5
sources.inspected: Sections 1 and 5 in the Elizabeth Carter translation hosted by MIT Classics.
supports: Distinguishing one's own actions/judgments from external outcomes.
Treating judgments about events as distinct from the events themselves.
sources.limits: Ancient Stoic philosophy. It is not experimental psychology and does not establish causal effect sizes for modern behavior change.

sources.author: Peter M. Gollwitzer
sources.title: Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans
supports: Implementation intentions link a specified situation to a goal-directed response in an if–then plan.
The research program examines how these plans can facilitate translating intentions into action.
sources.limits: Foundational 1999 article; it should not be treated as the last word on effect size or boundary conditions.

sources.author: Peter M. Gollwitzer & Paschal Sheeran
sources.title: Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes
supports: Across 94 independent tests, the review reported a positive medium-to-large overall effect on goal attainment (d=.65).
sources.limits: The literature and methods have evolved since 2006; use alongside newer synthesis.

sources.author: Paschal Sheeran, Olivia Listrom & Peter M. Gollwitzer
sources.title: The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests
supports: Across 642 independent tests, reported effects for cognitive, affective and behavioral outcomes ranged from d=.27 to .66.
Effects were larger when plans used a contingent if–then format, motivation was high, and plans were rehearsed.
sources.limits: Meta-analytic averages vary by outcome, sample and design; they do not guarantee benefit for an individual user or any specific goal.

sources.author: Benjamin Harkin et al.
sources.title: Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence
supports: Across 138 studies (N=19,951), interventions increasing progress monitoring also increased goal attainment on average (d+=.40).
Effects were larger when outcomes were physically recorded or reported.
sources.limits: Monitoring is a self-regulation technique, not independent verification of a person's action or inner change.
